projects.title: PONDULO
projects.desc: NISC 2026 winning team project: a touchless weighing prototype with ToF hand tracking, three STM32 controllers, a graphical interface and audio feedback.

detail.intro: Move your hand. Make a selection. Weigh a product. A physical interface that brings gestures, graphics and sensing together without touching a screen.
detail.recognition: One of three winning projects · NeaPolis Innovation Summer Campus 2026
detail.overview: PONDULO is a working competition prototype developed by Team 6 at the NeaPolis Innovation Summer Campus, associated with STMicroelectronics. It pairs a contact-free graphical interface with a physical weighing platform. A multi-zone Time-of-Flight sensor follows the operator’s hand, while three NUCLEO-G474RE boards divide sensing, interface rendering and weight acquisition.
detail.motivation: At a food counter, interacting with a shared keypad can interrupt the task of handling products. PONDULO explores an alternative: move a cursor in the air, pause to select an item and read its weight on the same device. The objective was to demonstrate an end-to-end interaction on real hardware, from hand movement to an on-screen cart and receipt.

workflow.title: Find a product
workflow.text: Move a hand in front of the ToF sensor to navigate the catalogue. Hold the cursor over a target for 1.5 seconds to select it.

workflow.title: Weigh it
workflow.text: Place the product on the platform. The scale node acquires and filters the load-cell signal; the interface receives the weight through an analog link.

workflow.title: Set the quantity
workflow.text: Use the touchless quantity keypad, with a PUSH-only entry to avoid accidental activation immediately after product selection.

workflow.title: Review the cart
workflow.text: Add the item to a cart and show an on-screen receipt. Context-dependent audio cues confirm key steps.

video.caption: The original team demonstration: hand navigation, live weighing and the on-screen retail workflow. Audio and labels are from the campus prototype.

architecture.intro: The prototype separates three workloads with different timing needs. Each board owns a subsystem; the display node brings their outputs together for the operator. Select a node to inspect its responsibilities and connections.

nodes.label: Sensor node
nodes.name: From depth to pointer
nodes.text: A data-ready interrupt and semaphore signal new ranging frames. The firmware maps the closest zone and admitted neighbours to a distance-weighted centroid, then smooths the cursor with fixed-point arithmetic. A separate pointer thread decouples cursor updates from sensor acquisition. A motion state machine identifies directional and depth gestures.
nodes.link: Output: ASCII $XY and $GS messages over USART3 at 921600 baud to the display node.
specs: Separate pointer update loop configured around 100 Hz

nodes.label: Display node
nodes.name: Where inputs become interaction
nodes.text: The interface uses uGFX on a 320 × 240 display. Pointer coordinates are retained as the latest state, while discrete gestures enter a mailbox. A graphics mutex coordinates rendering, with incremental redraws and cursor background restoration. The display also reads the analog weight and triggers the serial audio player.
nodes.link: Inputs: UART pointer/gestures + ADC weight. Outputs: SPI graphics + UART5 audio commands at 9600 baud.

nodes.label: Scale node
nodes.name: From load cell to live weight
nodes.text: The scale node reads the load cell through the HX711, applies a 16-sample moving average and handles startup tare, calibration and live/hold behaviour. It drives an independent eight-digit display, so the weighing subsystem has local feedback as well as an output to the graphical interface.
nodes.link: Output: 12-bit DAC on PA4 to the display node’s ADC2, with common ground. The exported range is clamped to 0–1000 g.

architecture.note: The rates above are firmware configurations, not measured end-to-end latency. The analog export range does not establish weighing accuracy.

approach.title: Smooth motion, separate timing
approach.text: Depth acquisition and cursor updates run independently. Fixed-point centroid calculation and smoothing make the pointer usable between sensor frames without implying new depth measurements at every pointer tick.

approach.title: State and events travel differently
approach.text: The display keeps only the latest pointer coordinates, while gestures use discrete mailbox events. This avoids treating a stream of positions and one-off actions as the same kind of input.

approach.title: Redraw only what changes
approach.text: Incremental updates and saved cursor backgrounds limit the area repainted over SPI. A shared graphics mutex coordinates screen transitions and cursor drawing.

approach.title: A simple analog weight link
approach.text: The scale exports weight as a DAC voltage and the display samples it with an ADC. This avoids packet decoding for that signal, but requires a common ground, endpoint calibration and a way to address the current lack of disconnect detection.

approach.title: Feedback beyond the screen
approach.text: The local digit display gives direct weighing feedback. A YX5300 MP3 module provides audio cues for presence, selection and receipt events.

validation.intro: The project reached a physical campus demonstration and was one of the three winning projects at NISC 2026. The repository also documents native tests and the boundaries of what they establish.

items.title: Implemented in the primary prototype
items.text: ToF cursor and gesture input, dwell selection, graphical retail navigation, physical weighing, local digits, an on-screen cart/receipt and audio command handling.

items.title: Software verification
items.text: Eight host-test executables cover cursor smoothing, gesture codecs and parsing, dwell/focus behaviour, audio events, JSON/cart models, storage fixtures and price-message validation. Mocks isolate software behaviour; they do not validate hardware timing or metrology.

items.title: A separate connectivity experiment
items.text: The ESP8266 web editor stores prices in LittleFS and sends updates to a standalone STM32 receiver. This receiver is not integrated into the main display firmware.

items.title: Demonstration boundaries
items.text: Clinical screens use sample patient records. Receipts remain on screen, and storage uses fixtures rather than a physical SD driver. No certified weighing accuracy, medical use or hygiene performance is claimed.

detail.outcome: PONDULO brought hand tracking, a graphical workflow and real weighing into one physical demonstration. The engineering takeaway is the connection between firmware and an interaction people can immediately understand: an input is sensed, communicated, interpreted and reflected on a real device.

nextSteps.title: Validate on hardware
nextSteps.text: Measure weight error and settling, check serial reliability under load, and inspect thread scheduling and stack usage. Consolidate shared ADC access under one owner.

nextSteps.title: Complete the price bridge
nextSteps.text: Integrate the standalone receiver with explicit price types and cart-update rules, then add acknowledgements, integrity checks and boot resynchronisation.

nextSteps.title: Make the build repeatable
nextSteps.text: Recover and pin the original ChibiOS/uGFX and toolchain revisions before claiming a reproducible embedded release. The repository preparation did not verify a full firmware rebuild.

detail.credits: Developed by Team 6: Alessia Giamundo, Emanuel Chirico, Federico Longobardi, Gianluigi Esposito, Lucia Cerullo, Matteo Saccone and Vincenzo D’Ambrosio. Team achievement at NISC 2026; repository maintained by Emanuel Chirico. Prototype photographs and demonstration video from the team presentation on Vincenzo D’Ambrosio’s PONDULO site.

projects.title: LUMA
projects.desc: Smart home prototype with two ESP32 boards running MicroPython: curtain control, keypad access, environmental sensing and ventilation, coordinated through MQTT.

detail.intro: A connected home, built at scale. Two ESP32 nodes bring sensing, access control and everyday automation into one physical prototype.
detail.overview: LUMA is a physical smart-home demonstrator built around a wooden scale model. The project connects everyday interactions—approaching the entrance, entering a PIN, moving a curtain and switching ventilation—to sensors, embedded controllers and visible mechanical actions. Two ESP32 boards run independent MicroPython applications and exchange commands and readings through MQTT.

approach.title: Entrance interaction
approach.text: The entrance node brings together ultrasonic presence detection, a matrix keypad, a horizontal OLED and a door servo. It provides local feedback and accepts remote door commands through MQTT.

approach.title: Environmental experiments
approach.text: The second node manages the stepper-driven curtain, light and temperature sensing, and the ceiling-mounted fan through a relay. The DHT sensor was placed outside the model so the team could apply a nearby heat source and observe its response during temperature tests. Separate upper and lower thresholds provide hysteresis in automatic curtain control.

detail.outcome: The prototype makes the complete sensing–decision–action chain tangible: physical inputs become readings, the firmware interprets them, and actuators change the model. Node-RED provided the original dashboard for remote interaction. LUMA remains an educational prototype; the project repository documents its firmware, MQTT interface and remaining engineering work.
detail.credits: Team: Francesco Apicella, Luigi Autorino and Emanuel Chirico. Technical description based on the LUMA repository; exterior DHT placement, thermal testing and ceiling-mounted ventilation clarified by Emanuel.

projects.title: Aequitas
projects.desc: Verifiable e-voting prototype with RSA-OAEP encryption, Shamir secret sharing and ballot inclusion receipts based on Merkle trees.

detail.intro: An academic exploration of digital voting: encrypted ballots, shared trust and individual proofs of inclusion.
detail.overview: Aequitas is an academic e-voting prototype built around a separation of responsibilities: voter authentication, encrypted ballot submission, ballot registration and tallying. It explores how cryptographic primitives can work together to make a voting process inspectable.

approach.title: Encrypted preferences
approach.text: RSA-OAEP protects ballot preferences before they are submitted to the ballot register.

approach.title: Distributed trust
approach.text: Shamir secret sharing splits the election key across trustees, requiring a threshold of shares for reconstruction.

approach.title: Inclusion receipts
approach.text: Merkle-tree proofs allow a voter to check that a ballot is included in the register.

detail.outcome: The prototype combines a Flask application with an inspectable cryptographic workflow. Google OpenID Connect acts as a stand-in for SPID during authentication. This is an academic proof of concept, rather than a deployed election system.
detail.credits: Team: Luigi Autorino and Emanuel Chirico. Summary based on the project README.

projects.title: VibeFlow
projects.desc: Desktop music player with a track library, playlists and interchangeable playback modes, built as a JavaFX team project using Command, Observer and State patterns.

detail.intro: A desktop music player used to explore how software architecture supports a changing, interactive application.
detail.overview: VibeFlow is a JavaFX desktop application for managing a music library, building playlists and playing tracks. The project uses familiar music-player interactions to put software design patterns into practice.

approach.title: Reversible operations
approach.text: The Command pattern records actions on the library and playlists to support undo.

approach.title: Playback behaviour
approach.text: State models player states, while Strategy provides interchangeable sequential, shuffle and loop modes.

approach.title: UI coordination
approach.text: Observer keeps interface elements updated when application state changes.

detail.outcome: The application brings library management, manual and automatic playlists, playback modes and undo into one desktop interface. The repository also includes project documentation and team development artefacts.
detail.credits: Team: Luigi Autorino, Emanuel Chirico, Chiara Crisci and Emanuela Graziuso. Summary based on the project README.

projects.title: SafeStep-XR
projects.desc: Hackathon project simulating industrial emergency shutdown procedures in virtual reality, with guided sequences, timers and immersive interactions.

detail.intro: An immersive training prototype for industrial emergency procedures, built during the Youbiquo hackathon.
detail.overview: SafeStep-XR uses Unity and C# to simulate emergency shutdown scenarios in virtual reality. Guided actions, time limits and feedback let the user move through a simulated industrial emergency.

approach.title: Guided procedures
approach.text: The scenarios combine sequential tasks, timers and visual guidance for activities such as isolation, cooling and evacuation.

approach.title: Immersive interaction
approach.text: XR interactions bring scenario selection, equipment manipulation and navigation into the virtual environment.

approach.title: My contribution
approach.text: Initial menu logic, supporting scripts, general integration and bug fixing, as documented in the team README.

detail.outcome: The hackathon prototype demonstrates procedural training in a simulated environment. Repeated-session reset and return navigation are among the improvements identified by the team.
detail.credits: Team project developed during the Youbiquo hackathon. Contribution summary based on the repository team table.

projects.title: Waste Sorting AI
projects.desc: Eight-class waste image classification with ResNet18 and ResNet50, exploring transfer learning, data augmentation, oversampling and fine-tuning.

detail.intro: Teaching a neural network to recognise eight waste categories, and exploring what changes when the training strategy changes.
detail.overview: This machine learning project compares ResNet18 and ResNet50 for waste image classification. The eight categories are battery, clothing, glass, metal, organic, paper, plastic, and undifferentiated waste. The project ranked 7th out of 54 university projects, achieving an accuracy of 71% on the test set.

approach.title: Transfer learning
approach.text: Pretrained ResNet models provide the starting point for classification experiments.

approach.title: Training experiments
approach.text: Oversampling, data augmentation and fine-tuning are compared across the two network architectures.

approach.title: Reproducible materials
approach.text: Notebooks, trained weights, dataset notes and a project report document the experiments and evaluation.

detail.outcome: The repository provides training and inference notebooks, final ResNet50 weights and an alternative ResNet18 checkpoint. Training was written for Google Colab and requires adapting the dataset and export paths before rerunning.
detail.credits: Team: Luigi Autorino, Emanuel Chirico and Alessio Ferrara. Summary based on the project README.
